source.title: Scale, Drivers, and Limits of Representational Alignment Across Large Language Models

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures representational alignment and explicitly qualifies convergence: global agreement can coexist with weaker local agreement, and alignment changes with input properties and comparison scale. It does not test alignment growth with model scale.
record.gate_note: The reported results are analyses of representational alignment across language models. The paper also discusses prior work, including scaling and cross-modal findings; those cited findings are not recorded as rows. The paper says its analysis does not test whether alignment increases with model capability.
record.test_reason: The study measures cross-model alignment among 16 language models. It shows that the score depends on the neighbourhood setting, the stimulus set and off-manifold inputs. It also shows alignment is far from complete: global RSA ≈0.53, local ≈0.10. It does not sweep scale or capability, and does not test causes such as shared data.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors also conclude three further things. For several phenomena, agreement rests largely on shared lexical content. It is selectively sensitive to logical scope and word order. Substantial agreement persists even for nonword lists, so shared geometry is not shared linguistic interpretation.
record.recipe_differences: The study introduces NW-RSA and CF-RSA and uses standard RSA plus Procrustes and linear predictivity for comparisons; it does not reproduce a model-scaling experiment. Its principal comparison methods and scope differ from the original Platonic representation hypothesis study.
record.method_sensitivity: Alignment changes with geometric neighborhood size and weighting; dataset; linguistic equivalence class; counterfactual phenomenon; paraphrase, scrambling, or word-list condition; and alignment metric. Layer-wise effects also vary with depth.

fits_no_version.finding: Counterfactual RSA: mismatching event roles, hierarchical syntax or discourse order barely lowers cross-model agreement. Changing logical scope lowers it from 0.43 to 0.18, with the same ordering under fixed Procrustes and linear maps. One-sided paraphrase gives 0.47 to 0.44; scrambling gives 0.22 and word lists 0.21.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Cross-model agreement on natural text rests largely on shared lexical content, though it is sensitive to logical scope and word order. This concerns what drives convergence, not its extent.

record.code_released: Not yet released; the paper says code and constructed datasets will be publicly released upon acceptance.
record.problems: The study does not test scaling with size or capability, and its open-weight model panel does not cover closed or substantially larger models. Stimuli are English-only and cover a limited range of constructions and topics. Counterfactual perturbations may alter multiple input properties. Most results are aggregate means over model pairs; several values are presented only in figures, and exact model parameter counts are not stated in the text.
record.rows_left_out: No additional numeric or text-described result bearing on the tested versions was omitted. Figure-only layer-wise curves are not separately itemized except where they directly support the fixed-mapping comparison; the text summarizes those trends in Appendix E.

untested.parts: No sweep over model size or capability. The authors say their analysis does not address scaling.
Intact-input Procrustes and linear-predictivity scores are shown only in figures, with no numeric mapping-loss claim. No stitching, relative representations or unpaired mapping.
No feature, neuron or SAE recurrence.
No calibration of the measures themselves; the metric comparison is in appendices only. No out-of-distribution test beyond the off-manifold text.
Whether alignment plateaus with scale, and whether shared training data or objectives explain it, are untested.

missing.what: Metric dependence of effect sizes: under Procrustes and linear predictivity, drops for scrambling and word lists are smaller than under RSA. The semantic, entity and task classes sit at or above the global sample.
Layer dependence: under RSA the entity class drops from above to below the global sample with depth. Off-manifold gaps change differently across metrics and layers.
Human-authored SWJN stimuli (Regev et al.) show smaller differences among word lists, jabberwocky and nonword lists than the generated stimuli do.
Intact-input Procrustes and linear-predictivity alignment scores, a possible bearing on V4 mapping quality. Figure-only, roughly 0.3–0.6.
Natural-sentence baseline RSA for the off-manifold experiment, needed for R17–R20. Figure-only.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V4 link and label are dropped. A fitted map is expected to degrade when inputs differ in meaning, so the counterfactual test does not bear on interchangeability. The reader's 'partial' states for R1/R2 were judged relative to the global ceiling; against V6 and V7 they show the effect fully. The study is not an original source. Model pairs are aggregated throughout, and there is no per-family breakdown.

versions.untested_parts: No sweep of model size, capability, or training scale tests whether alignment rises as models get larger or more capable.
No vision-language or paired image-caption representation comparison.
No comparison of same-architecture models across random seeds focused on shared features or subspaces.

Tests fitted Procrustes and linear-predictivity alignment on paired inputs, including fixed mappings under perturbations. Does not test stitching, relative representations, or mapping without paired data.
No recurrence of interpretable features, neurons, SAE features, or circuits is tested.

Tests dependence on geometric scale, linguistic stimulus set and perturbations, and alternative alignment measures. Does not test out-of-distribution generalization beyond the evaluated input conditions.
Tests whether alignment is incomplete and condition-dependent. Does not test whether shared training data or objectives cause alignment, or whether alignment plateaus with scale.

relationships.condition: Neighbourhood size or temperature in NW-RSA; corpus choice; syntactic equivalence class; off-manifold inputs given to both models
relationships.reason: Local NW-RSA is 0.10 against 0.53 global (R1–R3). Web corpora score above the Control sets (R4). The syntactic class scores 0.33 against 0.48 (R6). Word lists, jabberwocky and nonword lists score 0.38, 0.34 and 0.31 (R17–R19).
relationships.display_finding: Local NW-RSA was 0.10 versus 0.53 globally, web corpora exceeded Control sets, the syntactic class scored 0.33 versus 0.48, and word lists, jabberwocky and nonword lists scored 0.38, 0.34 and 0.31, respectively.

tranche.reason: The study qualifies broad convergence claims through weaker local alignment and sensitivity to linguistic inputs; it does not measure convergence trends with model scale.

source_check.notes: Each experiment has its own baseline; absolute RSA values are not necessarily comparable across experiments. The global RSA ceiling denotes the global comparison reference, not a measured reliability ceiling.

statements.correction: Equivalence-class RSA: semantic 0.50, entity 0.44, discourse 0.46, task 0.52; anchor baseline 0.48. Single-word substitutions: RSA about 0.48; smaller effect relative to their own natural-sentence condition; exact baseline unstated. Interpretation: limits_scope.
statements.problem: Selective robustness qualifies V6 rather than establishing its absence generally. Substitutions use a separate natural-sentence baseline, not the equivalence-class anchor baseline.
